headline: Five green ideas won $1.3M each. One is a country.
summary: Prince William handed out his Earthshot Prize in Mumbai on Tuesday: £1m, about $1.3 million, to each of five winners. Bhutan won for policies that guard water for 1.6 billion people across South Asia. Ørsted won for cutting its direct emissions 98%, coal to offshore wind. Mahindra won for electric rickshaws. William rode in one.

cover_question.q: Can a country win a prize?

cover_answer: Yes. Bhutan did, for guarding water for 1.6 billion people.
table_question: If you cleaned up a mess you made, do you deserve a prize for it?

5-7.script: A prince from England flew to India and gave out five prizes for taking care of the Earth. One went to a whole country, Bhutan, for keeping its rivers clean for the people downstream. One went to a company that makes little electric taxis with three wheels, about the size of a golf cart. The prince rode in one and said it was really good fun.
5-7.why: The rickshaw ride is the picture. The climate stays behind it.
5-7.why_long: A six-year-old takes one vivid thing for the whole event, so the script hands them a prince in a three-wheeled electric taxi, not emissions. Piaget's child this age reasons from what is in front of them: a golf cart they have seen, a prize they understand. Expect "can I ride one?" Not here yet. Mahindra wants a million in India.

8-12.script: The Earthshot Prize has five goals: clean air, clean oceans, less waste, fix the climate, protect nature. Fifteen finalists, five winners, £1m each to grow the idea. Ørsted ran on coal, switched to offshore wind and cut its emissions 98%. It's a science fair where the prize money builds the project bigger.
8-12.why: Five goals, 15 finalists, five winners, one check each: a chain.
8-12.why_long: At twelve a child is working out how systems reward people, so the script runs the chain: five goals, 15 finalists, five checks, and the money is for scaling, not spending. The science fair is a mechanism they have stood inside. Expect "why does a prince get to decide?" He doesn't alone. He started it in 2020. Judges pick.

13-17.script: Can a whole country win a prize? Bhutan just did, for water policy that reaches 1.6 billion people. Second: Ørsted won for cutting more than 98% of its direct emissions, and it got there by quitting coal. Does a company earn a climate prize for cleaning up what it burned?
13-17.why: A country as a winner, and a reformed polluter as one.
13-17.why_long: A thirteen-year-old can hold two true things at once: Ørsted burned coal, and Ørsted cut 98% of its emissions. The script asks them to weigh the past against the fix, the argument the judges already had. Kuhn calls that a practised skill; this is a case. Expect "will a prize fix anything?" Not alone. £1m each is seed money.

5-7.a: A small taxi with three wheels that runs on a battery instead of gas. The prince rode in one and said it was good fun.

8-12.q: Why give money to a country?
8-12.a: Bhutan's rules guard water for 1.6 billion people. The cash restores land.

8-12.q: Why did a prince start it?
8-12.a: In 2020, copying Kennedy's Moonshot: a huge goal, a deadline, a race.

13-17.q: Can a country win a prize?
13-17.a: Yes. Bhutan won for water policy that reaches 1.6 billion people.

13-17.q: Should a former coal firm get a climate prize?
13-17.a: The judges said yes: it cut direct emissions 98%. The past is your call.
